publication: The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures 48, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Augustine invents the philosophical concept of will (POLE 1: late, Christian, Latin, anti-intellectualist/voluntarist)
position_summary: The Greeks never developed a distinct concept of will, explaining human action through intellectual cognition and deliberate choice (prohairesis) rather than a faculty of will. The 'notion of will' as a tool of philosophical analysis (used from the early Scholastics to Schopenhauer and Nietzsche) was invented by St. Augustine, who reached it via Biblical anthropology (man as imago Dei), introspection, and Neoplatonic ontology. Paul had already implicitly introduced a notion of will distinct from intellect and emotion (grounded in obedience to God's commandment), but lacked any dedicated term for it; Augustine supplied the conceptual formalization. Dihle's notion of will is explicitly 'voluntaristic' (will as sheer volition irreducible to cognition) rather than 'intellectualistic'.
contested_locus: Augustine, De civitate Dei / De Trinitate / De libero arbitrio (voluntas as a distinct power of the soul); concept = voluntas / 'the will'
attested_quote: IT IS GENERALLY ACCEPTED in the study of the history of philosophy that the notion of will, as it is used as a tool of analysis and description in many philosophical doctrines from the early Scholastics to Schopenhauer and Nietzsche, was invented by St. Augustine.

publication: The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures 48, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Greeks never developed a distinct concept of will (supporting premise to POLE 1)
position_summary: Foundational negative thesis: classical Greek moral philosophy grounded human action in rational cognition of means and ends, attributing striving to instinct or emotion; the concept of choice (prohairesis) presupposes that intention depends on knowledge of something definite. There is therefore no Greek faculty of 'will' standing between belief and desire. This sets up the gap that Paul implicitly fills and Augustine terminologically formalizes.
contested_locus: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III (hekousion / prohairesis / boulesis); Greek term boulesis
attested_quote: IN THE TWO preceding chapters we came to understand why the Greeks, in their attempts to analyze and to evaluate human action, never developed a distinct concept of will.

publication: The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures 48, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Augustine = inventor of the modern notion of will (closing claim of POLE 1)
position_summary: On the last page of his book's main text Dihle restates the central thesis without hedging: Augustine is the originator of 'our modern notion of will'. Quoted here as transcribed by A. A. Long in his editorial notes to Frede 2011 (Frede 2011, p. 180 n. 3), who flags it as the sharpest formulation of Dihle's position against which Frede argues.
contested_locus: Augustine; concept = voluntas / 'our modern notion of will'
attested_quote: St. Augustine was, in fact, the inventor of our modern notion of will.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (ed. A. A. Long, foreword D. Sedley; Sather Classical Lectures 68, Univ. of California Press; lectures 1997-98, posthumous)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Epictetus / later Stoicism develops the first genuine notion of a free will (POLE 2: earlier, Stoic/pagan, Greek, rationalist)
position_summary: A free will is a technical philosophical notion with an identifiable historical origin, not a pre-theoretical belief humanity always held; neither Plato nor Aristotle had it. The first actual notion of a free will arises in later Stoicism, paradigmatically in Epictetus, by enriching the earlier Stoic theory of assent (synkatathesis) with a developed notion of an inner life and making prohairesis the locus of agency that no external force can compel. This Stoic notion is the ancestor that, translated into Christian terms, ultimately reaches Augustine — so Frede explicitly displaces Dihle's Augustinian origin backward to Epictetus. Frede's notion of will is 'rationalist' (will as the rational capacity to make the choices needed to live well), contra Dihle's voluntarist criterion. He notes the freedom is one only the wise person fully possesses.
contested_locus: Epictetus, Discourses (esp. 4.1, 'On Freedom'); concept = prohairesis / to autexousion / eleutheria
attested_quote: So here we have our first actual notion of a free will. It is a notion of a will such that there is no power or force in the world which could prevent it from making the choices one needs to make to live a good life or force it to make choices which would prevent us from living a good life.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (ed. A. A. Long; Sather Classical Lectures 68, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: The notion of a free will is an inheritance from antiquity with a datable origin (framing thesis of POLE 2)
position_summary: Opening programmatic claim: the notion of a free will is inherited from antiquity and was first thought in antiquity, but (unlike a perennial common-sense belief) it has a specific historical origin to be located. This frames the whole inquiry as origin-hunting — the very frame the KG meta-debate node marks as itself contested.
contested_locus: n/a (methodological framing of the whole debate)
attested_quote: The notion of a free will is a notion we have inherited from antiquity. It was first in antiquity that one came to think of human beings as having a free will.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (ed. A. A. Long; Sather Classical Lectures 68, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Explicit methodological disagreement with Dihle (POLE 2 vs POLE 1)
position_summary: Frede acknowledges Dihle's learning but states his aim is 'completely different': Dihle elucidates the origin of one specific (modern, voluntarist) notion of free will presumed to be 'our' notion, whereas Frede pursues a purely historical inquiry into when and why a notion of a free will first arose at all. He criticizes Dihle for passing over rival ancient notions (too 'intellectualistic', not 'voluntaristic' enough for Dihle's criterion) and proposes instead to identify the ancestor of Dihle's favored notion — which he locates in the Stoics, not Augustine.
contested_locus: Dihle 1982 (the rival thesis); concept = 'our modern notion of will' vs. the historical origin of any notion of free will
attested_quote: It seems to me that Dihle does indeed contribute a great deal to our understanding of the historical origins of a specific notion of a free will—one that is still quite widespread and that many may think captures the way we ought to conceive of the will as such. But my aim is completely different from Dihle's.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (ed. A. A. Long; Sather Classical Lectures 68, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: autexousion is Stoic in origin; Christian uptake begins with Justin Martyr (transmission claim of POLE 2)
position_summary: The term to autexousion originates in Stoic contexts (twice in the fragments of Musonius Rufus, then more often in Epictetus), spreads to Platonists and Peripatetics, and from Justin Martyr onward becomes very frequent among Christian authors. This grounds Frede's claim that Christian free-will vocabulary is inherited Stoic terminology, not a Christian invention.
contested_locus: Musonius Rufus, fr. 12 Hense; Epictetus, Discourses 4.1; Justin Martyr (terminus of Christian uptake); term = to autexousion
attested_quote: The term is twice found in the fragments of Musonius and then more often in Epictetus. It comes to be used by Platonists and Peripatetics but also from Justin Martyr onwards very frequently by Christian authors.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (ed. A. A. Long; Sather Classical Lectures 68, Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Origen inherits a basically Stoic free will, modified by Platonism not by Christianity (POLE 2 applied to Origen)
position_summary: Frede's chapter on Origen ('An Early Christian View on a Free Will') argues Origen integrates a basically Stoic doctrine of freedom (to autexousion) into a Platonist framework to combat Gnosticism and astral determinism. Where Origen differs from Chrysippus and Epictetus, the difference derives from his Platonism (e.g. identifying freedom with there being things up to us that can never be lost, so even demons retain it), not from his Christianity. Christianity's interest in free will was motivated by anti-Gnostic and anti-astrological concerns, so no radically new Christian notion was needed. (Frede thus reads Origen as a transmitter of the Stoic notion, not an inventor.)
contested_locus: Origen, De principiis III.1 (Peri autexousiou); contrast with Chrysippus/Epictetus and parallel with Alexander of Aphrodisias
attested_quote: Origen, unlike Chrysippus and Epictetus, but like Alexander, identifies freedom (to autexousion) with there being things which are up to you to do or not to do.

publication: Wege zur Freiheit: Menschliche Selbstbestimmung von Homer bis Origenes (Tria Corda 15, Mohr Siebeck)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Origen is the first to conceive libertarian self-determination systematically (POLE 3: between Stoic transmission and Augustinian invention; locates the decisive step in Origen, 3rd c.)
position_summary: Fürst traces the 'ways to freedom' (Wege zur Freiheit) from determinism through compatibilism to libertarianism. Early Christian Platonists of the later 2nd century first explicitly asked whether the decision (Entscheidung) itself is free — a question old Stoicism had not posed (it asked only about responsibility/attribution) — and answered affirmatively for every human being. This path led from determinism, through compatibilism, into libertarianism, which Origen 'then first systematically conceived' (erstmals systematisch konzipiert). The early Christian result is a 'christlicher Kompatibilismus' / 'kompatibilistischer Libertarismus' that receives Chrysippean compatibilist terminology but, against Stoic determinism and on Platonist grounds, advocates a libertarianism it cannot fully reach because of the deterministic strand of biblical compatibilism. Fürst pins the decisive figure to Origen, dated by his own works (Song of Songs Commentary c. 245; Commentary on Romans).
contested_locus: Origen, In Hieremiam homilia 18,3 (GCS Orig. 32, 154): τὸ γὰρ αὐτεξούσιον ἐλεύθερόν ἐστι ('for self-determination is free'); De principiis III.1 (Peri autexousiou); concept = autexousion / libertas arbitrii
attested_quote: Diese Wege zur Freiheit führten vom Determinismus über den Kompatibilismus in den Libertarismus, wie er von Origenes dann erstmals systematisch konzipiert wurde (Kap. V und VI).

publication: Wege zur Freiheit: Menschliche Selbstbestimmung von Homer bis Origenes (Tria Corda 15, Mohr Siebeck)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Early Christianity opens a new paradigm of freedom-thinking ('christlicher Kompatibilismus' / compatibilist libertarianism)
position_summary: Supporting thesis: early Christian philosophers propagated views on freedom that led into a new paradigm of freedom-thinking. Though their emphatic freedom-consciousness put them 'on the way to libertarianism', they had to combine it with a strongly deterministic biblical conception of freedom (God created man as a being of free self-determination, yet God 'determines everything for the completion of man'). The result is a Christian compatibilism that (a) receives the theorems and terminology of Stoic (Chrysippean) compatibilism, (b) on Platonist grounds rejects the attendant determinism (e.g. Epictetus's), (c) advocates a libertarianism, yet (d) never fully reaches it because the deterministic side of biblical compatibilism must be respected.
contested_locus: Irenaeus, Adversus haereses IV 37,7 (FC 8/4, 330); Clement of Alexandria (precursor); Origen (systematizer); concept = christlicher Kompatibilismus / Freiheit der Entscheidung
attested_quote: Das Ergebnis war eine Art christlicher Kompatibilismus, in dem (a) Theoreme und Terminologie des stoischen Kompatibilismus im Sinne Chrysipps rezipiert wurden, man sich jedoch (b) im Sinne vor allem der Platoniker vom damit einhergehenden Determinismus, wie er etwa bei Epiktet zum Ausdruck kam, abgrenzte und (c) mit der christlichen Betonung der Freiheit der Entscheidung einem Libertarismus das Wort redete, zu dem man aber (d) nicht wirklich gelangte, weil die deterministische Seite des biblischen Kompatibilismus zu berücksichtigen war.

publication: 'Freedom and Will: Graeco-Roman Origins', in R. Seaford, J. Wilkins & M. Wright (eds.), Selfhood and the Soul: Essays on Ancient Thought and Literature in Honour of Christopher Gill (Oxford Univ. Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: The idea of the will has four strands, all assembled only in Augustine; Epictetus does NOT anticipate it (POLE 1-aligned; direct rebuttal of Frede)
position_summary: Sorabji distinguishes four strands in the ancient idea of the will — rationality, freedom, power (will power), and perversion by pride — each found separately in earlier thinkers (Plato, Posidonius, Lucretius, Cicero, Plotinus) but assembled only in Augustine. Against Frede's claim that the idea of free will is already found in Epictetus, Sorabji urges that none of the four strands as a cluster is present in Epictetus: Stoicism has no 'will power' (only intellectual effort); Epictetus's free prohairesis is compatible with everything's having been inevitable, unlike the voluntas-freedom of Lucretius/Cicero and the Christian successors; and the will perverted by pride emerges only after Epictetus, in Plotinus. Sorabji concedes Epictetus's influence on later Greek Christians (Justin, Tatian, Origen) is on the idea of free will, not of the will.
contested_locus: Epictetus, Discourses (prohairesis); Augustine (the assembler); concept = 'the will' (four strands: rationality, freedom, power, perversion by pride)
attested_quote: In the ancient idea of the will Sorabji distinguishes four strands: rationality, freedom, power, and perversion by pride. Each of them is found separately in different thinkers before being assembled in Augustine. Against the recent argument by Frede to the effect that the idea of free will is already found in Epictetus Sorabji urges various considerations that distinguish Epictetus from Augustine, and argues that none of the four strands that make up the idea of the will are to be found in Epictetus.

publication: 'Discovering the Will: From Aristotle to Augustine', in J. M. Dillon & A. A. Long (eds.), The Question of 'Eclecticism': Studies in Later Greek Philosophy (Univ. of California Press)
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: The will is 'discovered' on a trajectory Aristotle → Latin voluntas (Cicero/Lucretius/Seneca) → Epictetus → Augustine; Epictetus a major authority (intermediate / developmental pole)
position_summary: Classical Greek philosophy has no distinct term or concept for 'will' as an independent faculty; Aristotle's hekousion, prohairesis and boulesis do not constitute a unified will. The Latin voluntas / libera voluntas emerges via Cicero, Lucretius (atomic swerve breaking necessity) and Seneca (libera voluntas as a technical term), and Epictetus's elevation of prohairesis makes him a major authority in the 'discovery of the will', possibly under Senecan influence, culminating in the Augustinian synthesis. H. Kahn, Discovering the Will...'). No verbatim Kahn quote is available, hence page=null and attested_quote=null.
contested_locus: Aristotle (prohairesis/boulesis); Cicero, Lucretius, Seneca (Latin voluntas / libera voluntas); Epictetus (prohairesis); Augustine (synthesis)

publication: 'Who Discovered the Will?', Philosophical Perspectives 6 (Ethics), Ridgeview, pp. 453-473
debate: Origins of the notion of will / who invents the will
stance: Aristotle already has a concept of the will (rational-desire / intellectualist), so it is not invented late by Augustine or Epictetus (dissenting 'no late invention' pole)
position_summary: Irwin surveys the rival candidates for 'discoverer of the will' (Romans; Augustine under Hebraic/Christian influence per Dihle; Maximus the Confessor; with Kahn 1988 cited) and argues against the consensus that the Greeks lacked the concept. Following Aquinas's reading, he holds that Aristotle's conception of boulesis (rational desire) just is a concept of the will — a third element in rational choice besides mere belief and mere desire. Critics who deny Greeks any concept of will really only mean they lack a *voluntarist* conception; but the intellectualism-vs-voluntarism dispute is a debate *between two views of the will* shared by disputants who both possess the concept. Hence the will is not a late invention; Aristotle already has an (intellectualist) concept of it. This directly opposes both Dihle (Augustine) and Frede (Epictetus) on the dating, and aligns with the position the KG attributes to Anthony Kenny (Aristotle had a theory of will, contra Frede).
contested_locus: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III (boulesis / prohairesis); Aquinas, Summa Theologiae Ia q80 a2 (reading boulesis as voluntas/will); concept = 'the will' as rational desire
attested_quote: if we admit that Aquinas has a concept of the will, and if we attend to his account of Aristotle, we must also attribute a concept of the will to Aristotle.
